Pilgrim and Stranger
PIL-grim and STRAYN-jer
noun phrase (theology)
From the KJV's "strangers and pilgrims on the earth" (Heb 11:13; 1 Pet 2:11); pilgrim from Latin peregrinus (a foreigner, one journeying through), stranger from Latin extraneus (one from without).

📖 Biblical Definition

Pilgrim and stranger is the Scripture's name for what the believer is in this present world: a sojourner passing through a country not his home, a foreigner whose citizenship lies elsewhere. The patriarchs "confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth" (Heb 11:13), seeking a better country, that is, a heavenly, wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God. Peter takes up the same word, beseeching believers "as strangers and pilgrims" to abstain from fleshly lusts which war against the soul (1 Pet 2:11). The Christian's home is not here. He holds the things of this life loosely, as a traveler holds the inn where he lodges a night, for his conversation — his citizenship — is in heaven (Phil 3:20), and he looks for the city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God (Heb 11:10). This is not a contempt for God's good creation but a refusal to settle down in a world under the curse as though it were the believer's lasting country. Bunyan made the whole of the Christian life a pilgrim's progress from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City. This dictionary confesses the pilgrim character of the Christian: he travels light, suffers as a sojourner, sets his affection on things above, and presses on toward home.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Scripture's name for the believer in this world — a sojourner passing through a land not his home, whose citizenship is in heaven (Heb 11:13; 1 Pet 2:11; Phil 3:20). He holds this life loosely, sets his affection above, and presses on toward the city whose builder is God.

PILGRIM AND STRANGER, noun phrase. The Scripture's name for the believer in this present world.

The patriarchs confessed they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth (Heb 11:13).

Peter beseeches believers as strangers and pilgrims to abstain from fleshly lusts (1 Pet 2:11).

The Christian's citizenship is in heaven (Phil 3:20); he seeks a better country.

Bunyan made the Christian life a pilgrim's progress toward the Celestial City.

📖 Key Scripture

Heb 11:13 — "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth."

1 Pet 2:11 — "Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul."

Phil 3:20 — "For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ."

Heb 11:10 — "For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The pilgrim character of the Christian is corrupted by a worldliness that sinks its roots deep into this present age, treating earth as home and heaven as an afterthought; and by a false otherworldliness that despises God's good creation and the duties of this life, forgetting that the pilgrim still has a road to walk and work to do along it.

expand to see more

The first corruption is to forget that we are pilgrims at all — to settle into the world, lay up treasure here, and live as though this life were the believer's lasting country. The prosperity preachers baptize this and call it blessing. But Peter calls believers strangers and pilgrims and bids them, as travelers, abstain from the fleshly lusts that war against the soul (1 Pet 2:11). The man who treats earth as home cannot help being entangled by it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, but a second and opposite corruption must be marked: a sour otherworldliness that despises the good gifts of God and the honest duties of this life. The pilgrim is not a hermit who hates the road; he travels it faithfully, loving his neighbor, working his calling, using the world without abusing it. The principle to recover is the right balance: our citizenship is in heaven (Phil 3:20), and we look for the city whose builder is God (Heb 11:10), yet we walk the pilgrim road with diligence and joy, holding this life loosely but not contemptuously, pressing on toward home.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the KJV's "strangers and pilgrims" (Heb 11:13; 1 Pet 2:11); Latin peregrinus (a sojourner) and extraneus (one from without) — the believer's status in this world.
